new_statements.rule_in_words: Drag-yab sMar is described as a restricted word-tone language, not a stress language: each word carries one of two lexically fixed tones (high vs. rising/low) realised over the first two syllables; syllables from the third onward are atonal (low level); some words additionally have an 'accent nucleus' after the first syllable (written with an apostrophe) which makes the second syllable atonal too. Suzuki et al. 2024 (pp. 67, 75, 79) analyse this as word-initial H/L register plus an optional accent nucleus, likened to Kansai Japanese, and state that a single-syllable stress analysis has not been applied and has no supporting realisation (said of Lamo, with the same framework applied to Drag-yab sMar). No source assigns word stress to any syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Suzuki et al. 2024 p. 75: in Drag-yab sMar 'the accent nucleus does not function in the numeral morphology'; tone of numerals differs by dialect (Table 4 p. 78: mBengo, Razi, rDzongsar). Suzuki et al. 2021 p. 192 (mBengo): in compounds each constituent morpheme may carry its own word tone, fixed per word.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word, citation forms from a ~500-item elicited wordlist; Razi dialect, Xiangdui Town, one male speaker in his sixties, recorded 2017). The same statement, verbatim, is given for Lamo and Larong sMar in the same article; the 2021 Japanese article gives the equivalent statement for the mBengo dialect (dPal-ri township) and the 2024 paper adds numeral-tone data for three Drag-yab dialects. Terminology: the authors call it 'word tone'; structurally it is a two-way register + accent-nucleus system (pitch accent-like), and they deliberately avoid 'stress'.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog drag1234 'Drag-yab' = Drag-yab sMar of Suzuki & Tashi Nyima (autonym m̥a55; Chinese Zesong 则松话 in Changdu Diquzhi 2005; Jiang 2022 lists 察雅 Mang 芒话 and Maji 玛吉话 varieties). The quoted statement is for the Razi dialect (Xiangdui/Byams-mdun Town); Suzuki et al. 2021 give the same system for the mBengo dialect (Bari/dPal-ri township), which is the area of Zhao's 'Dpal.ri Smar' (Glottolog maps Dpal.ri Smar to drag1234). Sister languages Lamo and Larong sMar (Zlarong) have separate Glottolog codes and are not covered by this statement.

new_statements.quote: The syllables in Dpal.ri follow the structure: (C1)(C2)(w)V(C3)+T, where C stands for a consonant, V stands for a vowel (either monophthong or diphthong), and T denotes a tone. [...] There are essentially two tones in Dpal.ri: high and low, and each has two allotones. The high tone is either high-flat or high-falling. The low tone is either low-rising or low-flat.7 [fn. 7: Tones are marked in accordance with IPA, with the exception of the low-flat tone, which is unmarked.] — and §1 p. 1: This paper concerns Dpal.ri verbs in Aorist and Factual categories. [...] The tone of a verb is marked as in Factual category (always on the last syllable).

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statement (Suzuki, Samdrup & Wangmo 2018: word-tone system, no stress statement) and with the catalog record, which has no rule. Adds a second dialect (Dpal.ri Township, 'Be.gzhi Village, Brag.gyab County) and a different tonal analysis: two tones high vs low with four allotones, versus Suzuki et al.'s high vs rising on the Razi dialect; plus the observation that the Factual verb's tone sits on the last syllable. No stress claim, so nothing to contradict on stress.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work treats Dpal.ri Smar as a tone language: every syllable carries a tone (T in the syllable template), with two tonemes, high (allotones high-flat, high-falling) and low (allotones low-rising, low-flat). It says nothing about stress, accent or prominence; the only placement remark is that a verb's tone in the Factual category is always on the last syllable, i.e. tone is assigned to one syllable of the word, but the paper does not frame this as stress.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; the paper is on person indexation and its phonology section is a two-paragraph overview only (searched the full text for stress, accent, prominence, prosody, suprasegmental, pitch: no hits beyond 'tone')
new_statements.identity_note: Zhao 2024 describes Dpal.ri Smar, the variety spoken in the northern part of Dpal.ri Township and in Rong.grub, Brag.gyab (Drag-yab) County, consultant from 'Be.gzhi Village 白西村 (Table 1, p. 3). Zhao treats Smar as four varieties (Dpal.ri, Rtsal.bzang, Zla.rong, Rong.smad); Dpal.ri and Rtsal.bzang are the Brag.gyab varieties that Suzuki et al. call Drag-yab sMar (Suzuki's Razi dialect and mBengo dialect are both in Dpal.ri Township), so the work is about the catalog's language, a different dialect from the Suzuki 2018 statement. Zla.rong corresponds to Larong sMar, a sister variety, not this item.

sources.note: §2.4 声調 p. 192 (mBengo dialect, dPal-ri/Bari township): 語声調で2種類が区別される：高 (ˉ) と低 (´)。声調を担う領域は語頭から2音節目までで、それ以降は弁別的な高さはなく、低平であることが多い。多音節語で1音節目のみに弁別的な声調が現れる場合、1音節目ののちに (’) で示す。一方で、複合語については、1つの語の中で成分（形態素）ごとに上述の規則が適用された声調を担うことがある。語ごとに決まっているようであり、表記 (’) は音韻論的に重要である。 [Two word tones, high and low; tone domain = first two syllables, rest non-distinctive low-level; (’) after syllable 1 when only syllable 1 carries distinctive tone; in compounds each morpheme may carry its own tone, fixed per word.] No mention of stress.

Reports, citing Suzuki & Nyima 2018: 'Tones are high and rising. The first two syllables of each word act as the tone bearing unit. The second syllable is occasionally out of the tone bearing unit.' Also lists Jiang Huo 2022 (Zhongguo Zangxue) and Changdu Diquzhi 2005 as naming Drag-yab varieties (Zesong, Mang, Maji). Nothing on stress.
